:::{#thm-riemann-general}
#### Equal-width Riemann sums converge to the integral

If $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ (@def-integrable),
then for every choice of the sample points $x_i^*$,
the equal-width Riemann sums (@def-riemann-sum-equal-width) converge to the integral:

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} S_n = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

:::

::: proof
The $n$ equal-width subintervals form a partition of $[a, b]$
whose mesh is $(b - a)/n$,
which goes to $0$ as $n \to \infty$.
So $S_n$ is one of the sums in the limit that defines the integral
(@def-riemann-integral),
along a sequence of partitions whose mesh goes to $0$,
and a limit that has the same value for every choice of partitions
has that value along this sequence too.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-riemann-equal-width}
#### Equal-width sums for $\int_0^1 x\,dx$

Let $f(x) = x$ on $[0, 1]$,
which is continuous and so Riemann integrable (@thm-cont-implies-int),
and take each sample point at the right end of its subinterval,
$x_i^* = i/n$.
With $\Delta x = 1/n$:

$$
\ba
S_n
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i}{n} \cd \frac{1}{n}
&& \text{(equal-width Riemann sum with } x_i^* = i/n \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^n i
&& \text{(factor out } 1/n^2 \text{)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{n^2} \cd \frac{n(n+1)}{2}
&& \text{(sum of the first } n \text{ integers)}
\\
&= \frac{n+1}{2n}
&& \text{(cancel one factor of } n \text{)}
\ea
$$

So $S_{10} = 0.55$, $S_{100} = 0.505$, $S_{1000} = 0.5005$,
and $S_n \to \frac{1}{2}$ as $n \to \infty$.
By @thm-riemann-general, $\int_0^1 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}$.

:::
